Lesson · 15 min

Trash, Storage, and Getting Files Back

Delete files safely, restore them from Trash within 30 days, know when a deletion is permanent, and keep an eye on your Google storage.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • ✓Move files to Trash and restore them
  • ✓Explain that Trash keeps files for 30 days and that Delete forever and Empty trash cannot be undone
  • ✓Explain what happens when you remove a file you do not own
  • ✓Check how much storage you use, what counts toward it, and which files use the most

Lesson Notes

Read through the key concepts before you try the challenge.

Trash is a safety net

On the job

You are cleaning up Parkview's My Drive.

My Drive is cluttered with copies of copies, an old flyer draft, and a huge lobby video. Yesterday someone deleted the Riverside pool rules by mistake, and Andre needs them back today.

Your task: Clean up without losing anything Parkview needs, and recover the pool rules.

  • Delete a file you own: select it and click Move to trash (the trash can) in the bar above the list, right-click › Move to trash, or press Delete.
  • Files in Trash are deleted forever after 30 days.
  • Restore: open Trash on the left side, right-click the file, and choose Restore. It goes back to where it was.
  • Delete forever: in Trash, right-click › Delete forever. Empty trash deletes everything in Trash forever.
Delete forever and Empty trash cannot be undone from Drive. Before you empty the Trash, look through it for anything a coworker might still need.

Files you do not own

Only the owner can delete a file. If you remove a file someone else owns, it disappears from your Drive, but the owner and everyone else with access still have it. To get rid of a shared file for everyone, ask its owner.

💡 Need an earlier version of a file rather than a deleted one? Open the file and use version history (File › Version history › See version history). Module 3 shows how.

Storage

  • A free Google account has 15 GB of storage, shared by Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Photos. A work account's storage is set by the organization's plan.
  • What counts: Gmail messages and attachments (including Spam and Trash), files in Drive such as PDFs, images, and videos, and items in Drive's Trash.
  • Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides files created or edited after June 1, 2021 count too. Files someone shared with you count against the owner's storage, not yours.
  • To see what uses the most space, click Storage on the left side of Drive, then click Storage used to sort by size.

When an account runs out of storage, you cannot upload to Drive or create new Docs, Sheets, or Slides files, and Gmail may stop sending and receiving. Deleting large files you no longer need, and then emptying them from Trash, frees space.

Challenge

Apply what you've learned in this lesson.

Practice in your own Drive with a file you do not need.

  1. Create a Google Doc named Delete Me and move it to Trash.
  2. Open Trash and find the message about how long files stay there. Write it down.
  3. Restore Delete Me. Check that it is back in My Drive.
  4. Open Storage on the left side. Write down how much storage you use and the name of your largest file.
Deliverable: Submit what you wrote down (the Trash message, your storage used, and your largest file) to your instructor or course folder. No Google account? Complete the practice simulation and submit its results page.
